hero.name: Farida
hero.who: a 41-year-old head chef in Bhopal who feels she must make every decision

story.b: Farida runs the kitchen of a busy hotel restaurant in Bhopal, and everyone knows she is the best cook in the room. She tastes every gravy, fixes every plate and decides every menu change herself. When she takes one Sunday off, the kitchen falls apart. Her sous chef Deepak calls her six times to ask about the biryani masala. The young cooks wait for her nod before adding salt. Orders back up, and two tables walk out. On Monday Farida is angry. She tells her husband she cannot trust anyone in that kitchen. Lying awake that night, she wonders why her team of fourteen seems to get less capable the longer she leads it.

ask.q: Farida's kitchen falls apart whenever she is away. What should she question first?
o: Whether she needs to hire smarter cooks
Whether her way of leading is making her team think less
Whether she should simply never take a day off
ask.why: New cooks would join the same kitchen under the same leader. Never taking a day off just hides the problem. When a team waits for one person's nod, the cause is often how that person leads. Questioning her own style is where Farida can actually change things.

chapters.take: If your team cannot think without you, look at how you lead.

story.b: Farida thinks back to her first job, twenty years ago, in a hotel kitchen in Mumbai. She had two bosses there. The first shouted corrections across the room and redid her plates in front of everyone. Under him she stopped thinking and simply followed. The second, an old pastry chef, once asked her, a twenty-two-year-old trainee, to design the dessert for a wedding. She stayed up three nights and surprised herself. She worked harder for him than for anyone, and she thought harder too. Farida realises, with a sinking feeling, which of the two she has become. At the next weekly meeting, Deepak shyly suggests a new marinade for the seekh kebabs.

ask.q: Deepak suggests a new marinade, and Farida's instinct is to say hers is better. What would a multiplier do?
o: Explain why her recipe is better, to save time
Accept it without comment to avoid any conflict
Ask him to test it on a small batch and share what he learns
ask.why: Shooting it down keeps Farida the smartest person in the room and teaches Deepak to stop suggesting. Silent acceptance gives him nothing to learn from. Asking him to test it and report back draws out his best thinking, which is how a multiplier makes the whole team sharper.

chapters.take: Some leaders drain a team's thinking. The best ones multiply it.

story.h: The new girl and the millet
story.b: Komal joined the kitchen three months ago, fresh from a catering college in Indore. Farida has kept her on onions, tomatoes and washing rice, assuming she needs a year before she can be trusted with anything real. One evening Farida notices Komal quietly tasting the staff dal and adjusting it, and it is noticeably better. The next day the hotel manager asks Farida for one new millet dish for a monsoon festival menu, due in three weeks. Farida's first thought is to stay late and create it herself, as she always does. Then she looks across the kitchen at Komal, chopping onions with her head down, and wonders what this girl might do if someone believed she could.

ask.q: The festival needs a new millet dish in three weeks. Who should Farida give the challenge to?
o: Komal, the new cook, with a clear brief and a deadline
Herself, since only she knows what really works
Komal, but only after a full year of chopping onions
ask.why: Assuming juniors cannot figure things out keeps them small. Doing it herself repeats the old pattern, and a year of onions teaches patience but not thinking. Believing Komal is capable and giving her a real problem, with a clear brief, lets her rise to it.

chapters.take: Treat people as capable, and they often rise to meet it.

story.b: Online reviews start complaining that main courses take too long on weekends. The old Farida would have announced a new rule at the briefing and walked away. This time she stands by the pass at four o'clock, before the dinner rush, and asks a question instead. How could we get main courses out in half the time? Silence at first. The cooks look at each other, waiting for her answer. She waits too, which is hard for her. Then Ravi from the tandoor says the kebabs could be marinated in smaller batches. The dishwasher, of all people, points out that clean plates are stacked at the far end, so everyone crosses the kitchen twenty times an hour. The argument gets loud and useful.

ask.q: Deepak now runs the breakfast shift, where egg orders are slow. What should he do first?
o: Announce a strict new timing rule for the egg station
Ask the breakfast team how they would speed it up, and let them debate
Cook the eggs himself every morning until things improve
ask.why: A rule from the top tells people what to do but not why, and doing it himself makes Deepak the bottleneck. Asking the team a real question and letting them argue brings out ideas only they can see, and people follow a plan they helped build.

chapters.take: A good question gets more out of a team than a good order.

story.b: Komal's millet khichda with smoked tomato chutney sells out on the first day of the festival menu. So when a family books the hotel for an eighty-guest wedding reception, Farida does something new. She gives the whole menu to Komal, from planning to plating, and tells her it is hers. On the evening of the event, Farida stands at the back of the hall. Komal has arranged the buffet in an order Farida would never choose, and the paneer is ten minutes behind. Farida's hands itch. Every instinct tells her to walk into the kitchen and take over. She takes one step forward, then stops by the dessert counter, watching Komal's face.

ask.q: Komal's order is running a little late, and she is doing things differently. What should Farida do?
o: Take over at once to make sure it is perfect
Leave the venue entirely so Komal is fully on her own
Offer a quick coaching tip if needed, then hand the work straight back
ask.why: Taking over at the first wobble teaches Komal the work was never really hers. Disappearing leaves her without help if things truly go wrong. Coaching briefly and handing the work back keeps ownership with Komal, and she learns to handle the pressure herself.

chapters.take: Hand over real ownership, coach when needed, then step back again.

story.b: Farida is proud of how the kitchen has changed. Then Deepak, over a late cup of chai after service, gently tells her something. She replies to every question on the kitchen WhatsApp group within a minute, so nobody else bothers to answer. And at the weekly tasting she always speaks first. Once she says a dish needs more salt, every cook suddenly agrees it needs more salt. Farida is stung. She thought being quick and clear was helpful. She thinks of last week's tasting, when Komal opened her mouth to say something and closed it again after Farida spoke. None of it was meant badly. But good intentions, she realises, can still make people stop thinking.

ask.q: At tastings Farida always speaks first, and then everyone agrees with her. What should she try?
o: Stay quiet for the first ten minutes and let others give their views
Speak first, but tell everyone they are free to disagree
Skip tastings so she does not influence anyone
ask.why: Saying people may disagree does little once the boss has already given her verdict. Skipping tastings removes her expertise altogether. Staying quiet first lets the team form and share their own views, and then Farida's opinion adds to their thinking instead of replacing it.

chapters.take: Even helpful habits, like answering fast or speaking first, can quietly shrink a team.

story.b: On a Sunday in December, Farida takes the whole day off and puts her phone on silent. When she checks it at night, there are no missed calls, only a photo of the service board with every order cleared. Deepak runs breakfast and has cut waiting time for egg orders, using an idea from the youngest cook. Komal now handles all outside catering and is training a new junior of her own. At tastings Farida speaks last, and she often learns something before she does. She still tastes the biryani masala, because some things are hers. But the kitchen no longer waits for her nod. It thinks for itself, and somehow that has made her a better chef too.

chapters.take: Great leaders are measured by how much their team can do without them.
